title: HR help desk software: Features, benefits, and what to look for
summary: Learn which HR help desk software features matter, how they reduce repetitive HR work, and what to look for when comparing platforms.
body_markdown:
HR support often starts with a shared inbox, Slack channel, or a mix of both. As a company grows, more employee requests come through those channels, and manually keeping track of who owns each one becomes harder. Requests can get missed, while others may receive duplicate responses because it isn’t clear who has picked them up.


HR help desk software centralizes those requests and streamlines the support process. It offers a range of features, including the ability to assign work automatically, and keeps confidential cases restricted to the right people. More capable platforms can even auto-solve routine HR requests.


This guide covers the features to look for, how they change day-to-day HR support, and what to ask when comparing platforms.


## TL;DR


- HR help desk software brings employee requests into one support process, making ownership clearer and reducing the chance that requests are missed.
- Once requests are captured and assigned reliably, automation can reduce the number of routine requests HR has to handle manually.
- Build your business case around measurable improvements such as less manual HR work and faster support. Also consider whether the employee experience becomes easier.
- When comparing platforms, check where employees can ask for help and how sensitive requests are protected. Then ask vendors what actions the software can complete inside connected HR systems.
- Risotto lets employees ask for help in the channels they already use. Routine requests can be auto-solved, while anything requiring HR input is handed over with the relevant context.


## Core features to look for in HR help desk software


HR help desk software captures, assigns, tracks, and helps resolve employee questions and HR requests. The right features should make requests easier to assign, reduce repetitive work, protect confidential information, and show where HR support time is going.


Here are the most important capabilities to look for.


### Automated intake and routing


The first capability to look for is automated intake. It can seem like a basic requirement, but it becomes more important as a growing company receives more HR requests across email, Slack, and other channels.


Automated intake captures those requests in the help desk so they can be categorized and routed automatically. For HR, that might mean a payroll question (along with the employee’s original context) going straight to the payroll team.


Automated routing reduces manual triage by sending each request to the appropriate team as soon as it comes in.


When comparing vendors, check which channels they can capture requests from and how routing rules are set up. Also ask what happens when the system can’t confidently categorize a request.


### SLA (service-level agreement) tracking and prioritization


SLA tracking helps HR set targets for how quickly different types of requests should receive a response or be resolved. Prioritization makes sure more urgent or higher-impact requests are handled first.


For example, a payroll issue affecting someone’s current pay may need to be triaged within a few hours, while a routine policy question can wait longer. Some requests may also have fixed deadlines, such as an HRIS change that needs to be completed before the next payroll cycle.


SLA tracking also helps HR spot requests that are close to missing their targets and see when unresolved work is starting to build into a backlog.


When evaluating a platform, check how flexible its SLA and prioritization rules are and how it surfaces requests that need attention. Also check what happens when a request changes queues or remains unclaimed, and whether the SLA continues to be tracked correctly.


### Role-based access and confidentiality controls


Confidentiality starts with where the employee asks for help. Sensitive requests such as leave of absence, employee relations cases, or investigations need a private route into the help desk rather than a public channel.


Once the request is submitted, access should also be restricted to the people authorized to handle it. Role-based access controls let HR decide who can view or act on specific requests based on the work involved.


This capability becomes especially important when HR and IT use the same[unified help desk](https://www.tryrisotto.com/use-cases/unified-help-desk) . Sharing a platform shouldn’t mean sharing access to every request.


Confidentiality should extend to the information the system uses to answer employees too. It shouldn’t surface restricted policies or information that doesn’t apply to the person asking the question.


When comparing platforms, check how granular the permissions are and whether that activity is logged.


### Employee self-service


Most HR help desk platforms offer some form of employee self-service, usually through a portal or searchable knowledge base.


That can work well when employees use it consistently. If they keep going back to email or Slack, however, HR still ends up handling those questions manually.


That means you should evaluate where self-service happens. Some platforms bring support into Slack, Teams, or other channels employees already use, so they don’t have to switch channels to request support.


Effective self-service should reduce the number of routine questions HR needs to handle directly, whether someone is checking a PTO policy, or looking for onboarding information.

### AI-assisted workflows and automation


AI-assisted workflows can reduce HR workload by handling routine requests from start to finish.


A PTO request is a good example. An automated workflow could identify the employee and retrieve their current leave balance. It could then collect the requested dates, ask the employee to confirm the request, and submit it to the HRIS. If approval is required, Risotto can submit the request to the HRIS, where the organization’s existing approval process continues.


Full automation won’t be appropriate for every HR request. For sensitive cases, HR may want the AI to collect the relevant information or prepare a response, then require a person to review it before anything is sent or changed.


For this type of automation, auto-solve rate is an important metric because it shows how often requests are completed without HR needing to step in.


When evaluating AI-assisted workflows, focus on what happens after the platform receives the request:


- Can it gather missing information and carry out approved actions in connected systems?
- Can you require human review for specific request types, and does the handoff include the context HR needs to continue?


### Integrations with HR and business systems


Integrations enable an HR help desk to work with the systems employees and HR teams already rely on, such as an HRIS, identity provider, or existing ticketing platform.


What matters is how much the integration can actually do. Some connections only let the help desk retrieve information. It might be able to look up an employee’s leave balance, for example, but HR would still need to complete any follow-up action manually.


Some integrations can also update the connected system or complete an approved action. For an access request, that could mean granting approved access and logging the change automatically.


When comparing vendors, ask them to walk you through a real workflow and show which steps the integration can complete automatically. The same applies to ITSM integrations: check whether the connection simply passes information between systems or can support the actions needed to resolve the request.


### Reporting and support analytics


When HR support is spread across different systems and channels, even basic questions about the workload can be difficult to answer.


Reporting functionality should break requests down by type and volume so HR can see where demand is coming from. It should also show how long different requests take to resolve, and what share of eligible requests are auto-solved without HR involvement.


That information can help HR identify the work that’s consuming the most time and decide what to automate next. It also gives leadership a clearer view of whether the help desk is improving support performance.


When comparing platforms, focus on the[help desk KPIs](https://www.tryrisotto.com/blog/help-desk-kpis) that reflect the outcomes you want to improve rather than the sheer number of[ITSM metrics](https://www.tryrisotto.com/blog/itsm-metrics) available.


## Build the business case around three outcomes


When you’re making the case for new HR help desk software, a list of features only tells leadership what the platform can do. Your business case should show what those capabilities could change for your HR team and how you’ll measure the impact.


Focus on the three outcomes below.


### Automate routine HR requests


Start building your business case by looking at the routine HR requests your team handles most often, and identifying which ones could be fully automated. Then estimate what share of those eligible requests a platform could resolve without HR involvement. That percentage is your expected auto-solve rate.


You can combine that with your monthly eligible request volume and average handling time to estimate how much HR time automation could save:


**Monthly eligible requests × expected auto-solve rate × average handling time = estimated HR time saved**


For smaller People teams, hours saved may not tell the whole story because request volume can be relatively low. In that case, you might also build the case around how consistently requests are captured and responded to within target times, or whether the platform could delay the need to add another HR support hire


For example,[Hazel Health](https://www.tryrisotto.com/customers/hazel-health-resolves-it-hr-tickets-79x-faster-with-risotto) reached a 35% HR auto-solve rate with Risotto. Using your own request volume and handling times, you can estimate how much HR time a similar auto-solve rate could save.


**Pro-tip:** If possible, establish your current request volume, handling time, and automation rate before rollout so you have a baseline to compare against later.


### Resolve employee requests faster


A second outcome to build into your business case is reducing how long employees have to wait for support. Start by looking at the request types with the longest resolution times, particularly when those delays hold up an employee’s work.


You won’t know the exact improvement before implementing a new platform, so use vendor results to understand what may be achievable.


Across Hazel Health’s IT and HR support, AI-handled requests had an average resolution time of 57 minutes, compared with 75 hours for human-handled requests, resulting in 79x faster resolution.


Use those results alongside your own resolution data to show leadership where reducing wait times could have the biggest impact.


### Improve the employee support experience


A third outcome to include in your business case is making HR support easier for employees to use. Look at where the current process creates friction.


HR help desk software can improve that experience by giving employees a simpler way to ask for help, and reducing the steps they need to take to get the right support.


This reflects the wider goal of improving the[ITSM experience](https://www.tryrisotto.com/blog/itsm-experience) : removing friction from the journey between needing help and getting the issue resolved.


For your business case, identify where employees currently have to switch channels, chase updates, or complete unnecessary steps, then show how the new platform could remove that friction.


After implementation, you can track employee CSAT and self-service adoption to see whether the experience improves.

## What to ask before choosing HR help desk software


Once you know which capabilities you need, use product demos and sales conversations to see how each platform would handle the HR requests your team deals with today. Here are some questions to ask vendors as you compare HR help desk software.


### 1. What percentage of employee requests can you fully resolve without HR involvement?


Not every “automated” request is actually resolved. A platform might answer a question, suggest a knowledge article, or route a ticket while still leaving HR with work to do.


Ask vendors for their auto-solve rate and, crucially, what has to happen for a request to count as fully resolved.


As we mentioned above, not every HR request should be fully automated, though. For sensitive or higher-risk cases, ask whether the platform can do the initial work while still requiring HR to review the response or action before it is completed.


### 2. Where do employees ask for help?


If the help desk requires employees to use a separate portal, but they still prefer Slack, Teams, or email, HR can end up managing requests in both places.


Find out where employees can actually ask for support and whether the platform works in the channels your workforce already uses.


### 3. How do you keep sensitive HR requests separate from routine questions?


A question about employee benefits and a confidential workplace complaint may both enter the HR help desk, but they shouldn’t have the same visibility.


Ask whether sensitive requests can be restricted to specific teams or roles, including within HR itself. Also check whether approvals and actions are recorded for later review.


### 4. What can the platform do inside our HRIS and identity systems?


Some integrations only let the help desk retrieve information from a connected system. Others can also update that system or complete an approved action.


For example, can the platform check an employee’s leave balance and then submit the PTO request? Can it grant approved access and set an expiry date?


Also ask how completed actions are recorded. If the platform submits a request or changes employee data, find out whether the HRIS shows who initiated the action and whether the platform acts as the employee or through a service account.


Where an HRIS doesn’t allow a particular change through its API, ask what the fallback workflow looks like.


### 5. Which metrics can we report to leadership?


Ask vendors what reporting is built into the platform and whether it covers the outcomes you included in your business case.


If your goal is to reduce manual HR work, look for reporting on metrics such as auto-solve rate and request volume. If faster support is a priority, check whether you can track resolution and first-response times. The important thing is being able to show whether the platform is improving the areas you used to justify the investment.


### 6. What happens when the AI can’t resolve a request?


Ask vendors to show you exactly what happens when a request needs a person. Find out what the employee sees, who becomes responsible for the ticket, and whether an escalated request can ever be closed automatically.


A reliable handoff should leave the request clearly owned by a human rather than depending on the employee to trigger the next step.

## Automate HR support where employees already work


As companies grow, HR teams have more employee questions and requests to handle. Without automation, that can mean more time spent answering the same questions, and handling routine requests manually.


Risotto helps take that work off the HR team’s plate. Employees can ask for help through Slack, Teams, or email, and routine requests can be resolved without someone needing to step in.


When a request does need human input, it can be handed over with the relevant context already attached.


For HR teams, that means:


- **Faster answers to routine questions.** Risotto can use approved policies, benefits information, and other HR documentation to answer common questions without employees waiting for someone in HR to respond.
- **Less manual work behind repeatable requests.** Risotto can handle the steps involved in requests like PTO automatically. It can check an employee’s leave balance, collect their requested dates, confirm the request, and submit it to the HRIS without HR manually processing the request.
- **Sensitive HR work stays private.** Confidential requests remain restricted to authorized teams, even when HR shares the same support environment with other departments.
- **No need for another disconnected support system.** Instead of forcing a replacement, Risotto can support HR alongside IT, Finance, Legal, and other internal teams, while working with existing ticketing or ITSM platforms.


The result is faster support for employees and less routine work landing on HR. By automating the questions and requests that don’t need human judgment, the team has more time for employee issues and people work that genuinely need their attention.
